> Does combining two measurements tell you anything that neither told you alone?
> This module shows how to check, surveys the integration methods, and argues
> that the simplest one is the baseline the others have to beat.

This module is a lecture and a discussion. There is no coding exercise. The
second half of the morning is your group presentations, given to one paired
group rather than the whole room.

## Running the analysis yourself

Nothing in this module is assessed, but the code behind every number on the
slides is short enough to read. The whole analysis is three logistic regressions
on a table with four columns.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(pROC)

# one row per participant: micro_z, host_z, preterm
per_person <- read_csv("per_person_scores.csv")

fits <- list(
  micro = glm(preterm ~ micro_z, per_person, family = binomial),
  host  = glm(preterm ~ host_z,  per_person, family = binomial),
  both  = glm(preterm ~ micro_z + host_z, per_person, family = binomial)
)

map_dbl(fits, ~ as.numeric(auc(roc(per_person$preterm, predict(.x), quiet = TRUE))))
anova(fits$micro, fits$both, test = "Chisq")
```

The two scores come from Tuesday and Thursday. One is the mean anaerobe fraction
per person from the species table, the other the mean inflammatory gene set score
per person from the gene table.

## Further reading

- [mixOmics](http://mixomics.org/), for canonical correlation, sparse PLS and DIABLO
- [MOFA](https://biofam.github.io/MOFA2/), for multi-table factor analysis
- [Modern Statistics for Modern Biology](https://web.stanford.edu/class/bios221/book/), Holmes and Huber
- [microViz documentation](https://david-barnett.github.io/microViz/), which we used all week
